content: Actinic cheilitis, also referred to as solar cheilitis or actinic cheilosis, is a chronic inflammatory condition of the lips caused by prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation. It is considered the lip counterpart of actinic keratosis of the skin and has the potential to progress to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). In actinic cheilitis, the affected lip typically exhibits thickening and a whitish discoloration at the junction between the lip and the surrounding skin. The vermilion border, which is the sharp demarcation between the red lip tissue and the adjacent normal skin, becomes blurred or indistinct. As the condition advances, the lip may develop scaling and induration. The lesion is generally painless and persistent, occurring more frequently in older males and individuals with fair skin who have a history of chronic sun exposure. Causes The primary cause of actinic cheilitis is chronic and excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation from sunlight. Additional contributing factors may include tobacco use, lip irritation, poor oral hygiene, and the use of ill-fitting dentures. Treatment Options Actinic cheilitis is considered a premalignant condition, as approximately 10% of cases may progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Since it is not possible to predict which lesions will become malignant, the current consensus is to treat all cases of actinic cheilitis. Treatment options aim to destroy or remove the damaged epithelium and include: 1. Topical Medications: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): This medication is effective for diffuse but minor cases of actinic cheilitis. It works by inhibiting DNA synthesis, targeting rapidly dividing cells, which accumulate the drug and undergo cell death. Normal skin is less affected. Treatment typically lasts 2–4 weeks, during which an inflammatory response occurs, followed by redness, burning, oozing, and eventual erosion. Therapy is discontinued when ulceration and crusting appear, with minimal scarring. Complete clearance is achieved in about 50% of patients. Imiquimod: This immune response modifier promotes an immune-mediated attack on tumor cells, leading to apoptosis. It activates macrophages and T-cells, causing epidermal erosion and potentially creating an immune memory that reduces lesion recurrence. Minimal scarring is observed, and complete clearance has been reported in up to 45% of patients with actinic keratoses. However, the optimal dose, duration, and long-term efficacy for actinic cheilitis remain to be established. 2. Procedures: Cryosurgery: This involves the application of liquid nitrogen using an open spray technique. Local anesthesia is not required, but treating the entire lip can be painful. Cure rates exceed 96%, making it the preferred treatment for focal areas of actinic cheilitis. However, adjacent tissue damage may delay healing and promote scarring. Electrosurgery: This alternative treatment requires local anesthesia, making it less practical than cryosurgery. It is effective for small areas but may also cause adjacent tissue damage, delaying healing and increasing the risk of scarring. Shave Vermillionectomy: This surgical procedure removes a portion of the vermilion ridge while preserving the underlying muscle. Significant bleeding may occur due to the vascular nature of the lip, and a linear scar may form, though this can often be minimized with massage and steroids. Healing time is short, and the procedure is highly effective. Carbon Dioxide Laser Ablation: This technique ablates the vermilion border and is relatively quick and easy to perform, though it requires a skilled operator and anesthesia. Secondary infection and scarring are possible, but scarring is usually minimal and responds well to steroids. Pain during the healing phase, which can last three weeks or more, is a potential issue. The success rate is very high, with few recurrences. Chemical Peeling: The use of 50% trichloroacetic acid has been evaluated, but results are generally poor. Healing typically takes 7–10 days with minimal side effects, but the success rate is reported to be less than 30%. In summary, actinic cheilitis requires prompt and effective treatment due to its premalignant nature. Various therapeutic options are available, each with specific advantages and limitations, and the choice of treatment depends on the extent and severity of the condition.
